chapter_summary:
Now that we understand the fundamental structure of the blockchain, let's dive into the individual units of value transfer: transactions, and how they are packaged into blocks. A Bitcoin transaction is essentially a record of value being moved from one or more Bitcoin addresses to one or more other Bitcoin addresses. It's not like sending a file; you're not actually "sending" bitcoins themselves, but rather transferring ownership of a record on the ledger. Every transaction has inputs and outputs. Inputs refer to the unspent transaction outputs (UTXOs) from previous transactions that are being used as funds. Outputs specify where the bitcoins are going, including the recipient's address and the amount, plus any change returned to the sender. Each input must be "signed" by the private key corresponding to the public key (address) that controls those funds, proving ownership without revealing the private key itself. This cryptographic signature is crucial for security and preventing unauthorized spending.

When you initiate a Bitcoin transaction using your wallet, it's first broadcast to the Bitcoin network. It doesn't instantly appear on the blockchain. Instead, it enters a waiting area known as the "mempool" (memory pool). The mempool is a collection of all unconfirmed transactions that have been broadcast but not yet included in a block by a miner. Think of it as a waiting room for transactions. From the mempool, miners select transactions to include in the next block they are trying to "mine." This selection isn't random; miners prioritize transactions based on the transaction fee offered by the sender. A higher fee generally means a higher priority for inclusion, especially when the network is busy and the mempool is full. This is a common mistake for beginners: assuming transactions are free or instant. Transaction fees are vital for incentivizing miners and securing the network.

Once a miner has gathered a sufficient number of transactions from the mempool (up to the block size limit, which is effectively 4MB in Bitcoin, though it's more nuanced with SegWit), they organize them into a block. To efficiently manage and verify all these transactions, a special data structure called a Merkle Tree (or hash tree) is used. All the transactions in a block are hashed, then pairs of hashes are hashed together, and so on, until a single "Merkle Root" hash is produced. This Merkle Root is included in the block header. The beauty of the Merkle Tree is that it allows for quick and efficient verification of whether a specific transaction is included in a block, without needing to download and process every single transaction in that block. It also makes the block header much smaller and easier to manage.

The block size limit is another critical aspect. Bitcoin's original design had a 1MB block size limit, which was a subject of intense debate and led to forks like Bitcoin Cash. While the effective block size has increased with SegWit (which optimizes how transaction data is stored), it still acts as a constraint. This limit, combined with the 10-minute average block time, dictates the network's transaction throughput. Understanding the interplay between transaction fees, the mempool, block size, and the Merkle tree is essential for comprehending how Bitcoin transactions are processed and confirmed on the blockchain.

screens.title: Transactions and Blocks: Packaging Value
screens.subtitle: How value moves as signed records, waits in the mempool, and becomes part of a block

narration.text: In this lesson we will treat transactions as the basic units of value transfer on Bitcoin, and blocks as the containers that make those transfers permanent. You will learn what a transaction actually is, why it uses inputs and outputs rather than moving coins, and how signatures prove permission to spend. We will follow a transaction from creation in your wallet, through broadcast into the mempool, and through miner selection into a mined block. Along the way we explain the incentives that fees create and the engineering that keeps verification efficient, including Merkle Trees and the Merkle Root in the block header. Understanding these pieces helps you avoid common misconceptions: transactions are records of ownership change, not literal packets of coins, and confirmations depend on miners and fees, not instant propagation alone. By the end you will be able to identify inputs, outputs, the role of UTXOs, why fees matter during congestion, and how a Merkle Root proves a transaction’s inclusion. Think of this chapter as both a mental model and a practical map: you can use it to read a transaction on a block explorer and to reason about confirmation times and security.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Bitcoin transactions change ownership of UTXOs with signed inputs and outputs; miners collect transactions from the mempool, prioritize by fees, and summarize them with a Merkle Root inside a block.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These learning objectives map to practical, verifiable skills. First, you will describe the lifecycle of a Bitcoin transaction from creation to inclusion in a block. That means explaining how a wallet builds a transaction, how it is broadcast, what the mempool is, and how miners select transactions. Second, you will explain how miners group transactions and organize them within a block, including the role of the Merkle Tree and the Merkle Root. Third, you will identify the key components of a transaction: inputs that reference UTXOs, outputs that assign value to addresses including change, and signatures that authorize spending. Finally, you will understand the mempool and transaction fees: why fees are offered, how miners prioritize by fee per byte or weight, and the consequences of network congestion. Each objective matters because these are the concepts you will use when you read a block explorer, estimate confirmation times, or reason about transaction security. As you study, check that you can explain each item in your own words and point to a concrete example on a block explorer or in a wallet.

screens.title: What is a Bitcoin Transaction?
screens.subtitle: A signed record that transfers ownership of UTXOs

narration.text: A Bitcoin transaction is a signed record broadcast to the network that reallocates ownership of prior unspent transaction outputs, called UTXOs. It is not a package of coins shipped across a network; instead it updates who controls specific UTXOs on the ledger. Each transaction lists one or more inputs and one or more outputs. Inputs point to UTXOs created by earlier transactions and must be authorized with cryptographic signatures. Outputs assign amounts to recipient addresses and may include a change output that returns leftover value back to the sender. This model enforces conservation of value: the total of inputs equals the total of outputs plus any fee. A practical example is when your wallet builds a transaction that spends a UTXO of 0.8 BTC, sends 0.1 BTC to a friend, and returns 0.698 BTC as change, leaving 0.002 BTC as a fee. A common beginner misconception is to think addresses hold balances like a bank account; instead, balance is the sum of your unspent outputs, and spending consumes those outputs. Understanding this definition helps you parse raw transactions on an explorer and reason about why signatures and exact inputs matter.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A transaction is a signed instruction that spends previous UTXOs and creates new outputs, preserving total value.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › What is a Bitcoin Transaction?
Definition
Transaction as a signed record
A transaction consumes previous unspent outputs and creates new outputs. Inputs must be authorized with signatures and outputs specify recipient addresses and amounts.
Input = reference to UTXO + signature
Output = recipient address + amount (plus change)
Fee = inputs − outputs
Concrete example
Imagine spending a UTXO worth 0.8 BTC: send 0.1 BTC to a friend, return 0.698 BTC as change, leave 0.002 BTC as fee. Inputs must match total outputs plus fee.
Common misconception
Addresses are not accounts. Your balance is the sum of UTXOs you control. Spending consumes UTXOs and creates new ones.
Key Takeaway

Transactions reassign ownership by consuming UTXOs and creating outputs; signatures prove permission to spend.

screens.title: Inputs, Outputs, and UTXOs
screens.subtitle: How previous outputs become spendable inputs and how change works

narration.text: Inputs and outputs form a hierarchy of value movement. An output created by a past transaction becomes a UTXO — an unspent transaction output — that a later transaction references as an input. Each input contains a pointer to that previous output and a signature proving the spender controls the address tied to the UTXO. Outputs list a destination address and an amount. Wallets often construct transactions that spend one or more UTXOs and produce one or more outputs: some outputs are payments, and one is commonly the change returned to the sender. This pattern means that a single small payment may consume a larger UTXO and produce a new UTXO for change. A practical misunderstanding is thinking a wallet reduces a single account balance; instead a wallet selects UTXOs to cover the payment and fee. When learning to read transaction details, check the inputs list to see where funds came from, inspect outputs to find recipients and change, and verify that sum(inputs) equals sum(outputs) plus the fee — that's conservation of value in action. Inputs, Outputs, and UTXOs means utxos are outputs that can be spent later; inputs reference those utxos and require signatures. change is a normal output back to the sender.. In practical terms, how previous outputs become spendable inputs and how change works. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: UTXO model
keyIdea.text: UTXOs are outputs that can be spent later; inputs reference those UTXOs and require signatures. Change is a normal output back to the sender.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Inputs, Outputs, and UTXOs
Hierarchy
Inputs ← UTXOs ← Outputs
Outputs created by transactions become UTXOs, which later transactions reference as inputs. Wallets select UTXOs to fund new outputs and fees.
Select UTXOs to cover payment + fee
Create outputs for recipient and change
Sign inputs to authorize spending
Concrete scenario
Your wallet spends a single UTXO of 1 BTC to send 0.25 BTC. It creates two outputs: 0.25 BTC to the recipient and 0.749 BTC back to you as change, with 0.001 BTC as fee. The original UTXO is now spent and no longer available.
Misconception
Don't assume balances are single numbers stored on-chain. Balances are computed from the set of UTXOs you control.
Key Takeaway

Inputs spend UTXOs; outputs create new UTXOs. Change is simply an output back to the sender.

screens.title: From Wallet to Mempool
screens.subtitle: How a transaction is broadcast and waits for inclusion

narration.text: When you create a transaction in your wallet, it does not immediately become part of the blockchain. Instead the wallet constructs inputs, outputs, and signatures, then broadcasts the transaction to connected peers. Each receiving node verifies syntax, checks that referenced UTXOs are unspent, and validates signatures. If valid, the node places the transaction into its mempool — a temporary holding area for unconfirmed transactions. The mempool is not a single global queue but a collection of each node's view of pending transactions. Miners pull transactions from their mempool when building blocks. Fees matter here: miners are economically motivated to include higher-fee transactions first, especially under congestion. A typical learner error is assuming broadcast equals confirmation; instead broadcast merely shares the transaction and puts it into mempools. Also, if a transaction offers a very low fee it may remain in mempools for a long time or be dropped. Practically, you can watch a transaction propagate by observing its appearance in different node or explorer mempools, and check the fee per byte to anticipate how quickly miners will choose it. From Wallet to Mempool means the mempool holds valid, unconfirmed transactions; miners select from their mempool and prioritize by fee during block construction.. In practical terms, how a transaction is broadcast and waits for inclusion. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Mempool role
keyIdea.text: The mempool holds valid, unconfirmed transactions; miners select from their mempool and prioritize by fee during block construction.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › From Wallet to Mempool
Process Flow
Build → Broadcast → Validate → Mempool
  1. Wallet assembles inputs, outputs, and signatures.
  2. Transaction is announced to connected peer nodes.
  3. Nodes validate syntax, signatures, and UTXO availability.
  4. Valid transactions enter node mempools awaiting mining.
Why fees matter: miners choose higher-fee transactions first.
Watch out: low-fee transactions may be delayed or dropped.
Concrete example
Your wallet broadcasts a signed transaction. Nodes check the signature and referenced UTXOs. If valid, the transaction appears in mempools across nodes. A miner inspecting its mempool orders pending transactions by fee per byte when assembling a candidate block.
Misconception
Broadcasting does not guarantee mining; confirmation requires that a miner include the transaction in a mined block.
Key Takeaway

The mempool is a temporary queue of validated, unconfirmed transactions; miners select from it using fee incentives.

screens.title: Miner Selection and Transaction Fees
screens.subtitle: Why miners prioritize by fee and how it affects confirmation time

narration.text: Miners select transactions from their mempool when constructing a block, and fees are the primary economic signal guiding that selection. Each transaction includes an implied fee: the difference between the sum of its inputs and the sum of its outputs. Because block space is limited, especially under contention, miners naturally prioritize transactions offering a higher fee per byte or per weight unit to maximize revenue. This means that during busy periods, a low-fee transaction may take many blocks to be confirmed, and some may be dropped from mempools. A common student mistake is assuming transactions are first-come, first-served. In practice, miners sort by expected reward per byte. That makes transaction size relevant: a large, low-fee transaction is less attractive than a compact, higher-fee transaction that yields the same total fee. Practically, when sending value, adjust the fee estimate to current network conditions: use fee estimates provided by wallets or observe mempool fee ranges. The economic mechanism aligns miner incentives with network service by rewarding those who include high-fee transactions. Miner Selection and Transaction Fees means miners prioritize transactions by fee per byte/weight because block space is limited; transaction size and fee determine priority.. In practical terms, why miners prioritize by fee and how it affects confirmation time. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Fee priority
keyIdea.text: Miners prioritize transactions by fee per byte/weight because block space is limited; transaction size and fee determine priority.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Miner Selection & Fees
Comparison
High fee per byte vs Low fee per byte
Miners rank transactions by expected reward per byte. A higher fee per byte typically yields earlier inclusion.
Higher fee per byte → faster inclusion
Larger transactions need higher fees to be competitive
Low-fee txs may be delayed or dropped during congestion
Concrete example
Two transactions enter a mempool: a compact one paying a moderate fee per byte, and a large one paying the same total fee but lower fee per byte. Miners will usually include the compact higher-fee-per-byte transaction first because it maximizes fee income per block space.
Misconception
Assuming miners include transactions in chronological order is incorrect; miners maximize fee revenue when choosing transactions.
Key Takeaway

Fee per byte is the main priority signal; choose fees according to current mempool pressure to control confirmation time.

screens.title: How Miners Package Transactions into Blocks
screens.subtitle: Collecting transactions up to the block size limit and preparing the header

narration.text: When a miner prepares to mine a block, they collect transactions from their mempool into a candidate block. They include as many high-priority transactions as will fit within the block size or weight limit. Traditionally Bitcoin had a 1MB block size limit; effective limits have evolved with SegWit optimizations, and practitioners sometimes describe an effective limit around 4MB in terms of weight units, acknowledging SegWit's different counting rules. Once the miner selects transactions, they compute the Merkle Root summarizing all transaction hashes and place that root into the block header along with a timestamp, version, previous block hash, and a nonce field they will vary while attempting to find a valid proof-of-work. Packing efficiently matters: miners aim to maximize fee revenue per block while respecting protocol size constraints. A frequent mistake is to imagine unlimited transaction inclusion; block size and average block time — about ten minutes — together limit throughput and shape fee markets. Understanding this packaging explains why blocks have finite capacity and why fees rise during demand spikes. How Miners Package Transactions into Blocks means miners assemble transactions to fit within the block size/weight limit, compute a merkle root, and include it in the block header before mining.. In practical terms, collecting transactions up to the block size limit and preparing the header. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Block packaging
keyIdea.text: Miners assemble transactions to fit within the block size/weight limit, compute a Merkle Root, and include it in the block header before mining.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › How Miners Package Transactions
Architecture
Select → Pack → Header → Mine
Miners choose transactions up to the block weight limit, compute the Merkle Root, build the block header, and then search for a valid nonce.
Select highest-fee-per-byte transactions first
Compute Merkle Root for all transactions
Include Merkle Root in the block header
Concrete note
Block size limits constrain how many transactions fit per block. SegWit changed how weight is counted, increasing effective capacity while preserving protocol rules about what miners include in a header.
Misconception
Blocks are not unlimited. Throughput depends on block weight/size and the ten-minute average block interval, which together shape fees during high demand.
Key Takeaway

Miners optimize block contents to maximize fees while respecting size constraints; the Merkle Root in the header summarizes included transactions.

screens.title: Merkle Tree and Merkle Root
screens.subtitle: Efficiently proving a transaction’s inclusion without downloading the whole block

narration.text: The Merkle Tree is a hash tree built from all transactions in a block to produce a single fingerprint called the Merkle Root. Each transaction is hashed, then pairs of hashes are combined and hashed together up the tree until a single root hash remains. That Merkle Root is placed in the block header, and it allows lightweight clients to verify inclusion of an individual transaction without downloading the full block. A client needs only the transaction hash and the small set of intermediate hashes that form a path to the Merkle Root — this is called a Merkle proof. The security benefit is immediate: if anyone tampers with a transaction, its leaf hash changes and that will propagate up the tree and change the Merkle Root, making tampering obvious. A common novice question is why we need Merkle Trees if miners already include all transactions: the answer is efficiency for verification by remote or resource-limited clients. Merkle Trees make proofs small and verification much faster while keeping the block header compact. Merkle Tree and Merkle Root means a merkle tree summarizes all transactions into one merkle root, enabling compact inclusion proofs without downloading full blocks.. In practical terms, efficiently proving a transaction’s inclusion without downloading the whole block. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Merkle Tree
keyIdea.text: A Merkle Tree summarizes all transactions into one Merkle Root, enabling compact inclusion proofs without downloading full blocks.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Merkle Tree & Merkle Root
Definition
Leaf hashes → paired hashes → Merkle Root
Hash all transactions, combine pairs iteratively, and derive a single Merkle Root. This root is stored in the block header and represents all transactions compactly.
Compact inclusion proofs for light clients
Tampering changes the root, providing integrity checks
Small Merkle paths are efficient to transmit and verify
Concrete explanation
If you hold a transaction hash and the small set of sibling hashes up the tree, you can recompute the Merkle Root and confirm the transaction is part of the block header without downloading every transaction.
Misconception
Merkle Trees are not about compression of transaction data for storage; they are about efficient, verifiable summaries that enable inclusion proofs.
Key Takeaway

The Merkle Root gives a compact, tamper-evident fingerprint of all transactions in a block, enabling lightweight verification.

screens.title: Sending vs Ownership Transfer
screens.subtitle: Why transactions transfer ownership of UTXOs rather than moving coins

narration.text: People often say they 'sent bitcoins' as if moving a file from one computer to another. In Bitcoin's UTXO model, what actually happens is a transfer of ownership: the ledger records that specific UTXOs are now spendable by a different public key or address. There is no physical coin moving. This distinction matters for reasoning about privacy, change addresses, and wallet behavior. For example, spending a UTXO creates new outputs; one of those may be change that returns leftover funds to your wallet under a different address. Understanding ownership transfer clarifies why wallets consolidate UTXOs, why fee estimation depends on which UTXOs are spent, and why reuse of addresses can harm privacy. A common mistake is to treat addresses like account balances; instead treat them as labels for outputs. In practice, when you examine a transaction, ask which outputs are likely the recipient and which are change. This helps you confirm that a payment actually moved value to the intended party while preserving the ledger’s conservation of value. Sending vs Ownership Transfer means transactions change control of utxos; coins are not moved, ownership records are updated via spent inputs and created outputs.. In practical terms, why transactions transfer ownership of utxos rather than moving coins. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Ownership model
keyIdea.text: Transactions change control of UTXOs; coins are not moved, ownership records are updated via spent inputs and created outputs.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Sending vs Ownership Transfer
Comparison
Sending coins vs Changing ownership
Instead of moving coins, transactions reassign which public key can spend a UTXO. New outputs represent newly owned UTXOs.
Recipient output ≈ new UTXO controlled by recipient
Change output ≈ new UTXO controlled by sender
Inputs are spent and no longer available
Practical pointer
When reading a TxID, the largest output is not always the recipient; sometimes the change output looks similar in size. Identifying change often requires reasoning about where the sender controls an address.
Misconception
Don't assume addresses are account ledgers. Instead, track UTXOs and the addresses that control them to understand where funds moved.
Key Takeaway

Transactions update ownership of UTXOs; reading outputs carefully helps you identify recipients and change addresses.

screens.title: Lifecycle Walkthrough: End-to-End
screens.subtitle: Follow a transaction from wallet creation to block confirmation

narration.text: Let's walk through a typical transaction lifecycle step by step to synthesize the previous material. Step one: a wallet selects UTXOs sufficient to cover the payment and estimated fee, constructs outputs for the recipient and change, and signs the inputs with private keys. Step two: the wallet broadcasts the signed transaction to connected peers. Step three: nodes validate the transaction and place it into their mempools if it passes checks. Step four: miners sample their mempool, prioritize by fee per byte, and assemble a candidate block up to the size or weight limit. Step five: miners compute the Merkle Root for the candidate's transactions and insert it into the block header. Step six: a miner finds a valid proof-of-work and broadcasts the mined block. Other nodes validate the block and its transactions and then the block's transactions gain their first confirmation. A practical contrast: a transaction stuck with low fees can stay in mempools for many blocks or be dropped, which shows why fee selection is part of wallet design. As a reflective question, when you build a transaction, which step gives you the most control over confirmation speed?

keyIdea.title: Lifecycle steps
keyIdea.text: Build, broadcast, mempool validation, miner selection, Merkle Root computation, mining, block validation, and confirmations.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Lifecycle Walkthrough
Code-style Walkthrough
// Pseudocode lifecycle (conceptual)
wallet.buildTransaction(inputs, outputs)
wallet.signInputs(privateKeys)
network.broadcast(signedTransaction)
node.validate(signedTransaction)
node.mempool.add(signedTransaction)
miner.selectTransactions(mempool)
miner.computeMerkleRoot(selectedTransactions)
miner.mineBlock(headerWithMerkleRoot)
network.broadcast(minedBlock)
node.validate(minedBlock)
// transactions get first confirmation
This pseudocode shows the key steps in sequence without platform-specific APIs. It emphasizes where validation, mempool handling, and mining occur.
Example scenario
You create and sign a transaction, watch it appear in explorers as unconfirmed, and then observe a mined block where the transaction receives its first confirmation. If fees are low, you may see it remain unconfirmed for many blocks.
Misconception
Signing a transaction and broadcasting it are separate from it being mined; only inclusion in a validated block yields confirmation.
Key Takeaway

You control inputs and fee; miners control inclusion. The lifecycle steps show where choices affect confirmation times and finality.

screens.title: Block Size Limit and Throughput
screens.subtitle: How limits and average block time shape transaction capacity

narration.text: Block size and weight limits are fundamental constraints on how many transactions the Bitcoin network can process per block. Historically Bitcoin had a one-megabyte block limit. With SegWit, the way data is counted changed and effective capacity in weight units increased, which practitioners sometimes describe as an effective limit near four megabytes in certain measures. The point for learners is this: blocks are finite, and together with the average block interval — roughly ten minutes — they determine network throughput. When demand exceeds capacity, the mempool grows and fees rise because users compete for limited space. This supply-and-demand interaction is what creates the fee market. A common misunderstanding is that increasing fees immediately speeds confirmation regardless of block limits; fees influence miner selection, but block capacity still caps how many transactions can be confirmed every ten minutes. Understanding limits helps you reason about why fees spike during congestion and why scaling debates revolve around how to increase throughput safely. Block Size Limit and Throughput means block size/weight limits and the average block interval create a throughput ceiling that gives rise to fee markets under high demand.. In practical terms, how limits and average block time shape transaction capacity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Capacity constraint
keyIdea.text: Block size/weight limits and the average block interval create a throughput ceiling that gives rise to fee markets under high demand.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Block Size Limit & Throughput
Definition
Limits → throughput → fee market
Block size or weight limits restrict total transaction data per block. The ten-minute average block time together with this limit sets maximum network throughput, shaping the fee market during demand spikes.
Limited space means competition when demand rises
SegWit changes counting rules and increases effective capacity
Throughput limits explain why fees spike under heavy usage
Concrete insight
Because block space is scarce over each ten-minute interval, fee bidding emerges: users attach higher fees to reduce waiting. This mechanism aligns miner incentives with demand for confirmation.
Misconception
Higher fees do not expand block capacity; they only change ordering of transactions competing for limited space.
Key Takeaway

Block limits plus average block time set throughput; fees coordinate user demand for that limited space.

narration.text: This activity practices reading a real transaction with the goal of identifying its components and reasoning about confirmations. Use a block explorer to find a recent confirmed transaction. Locate the TxID, then check status: how many confirmations does it have? Next inspect the amount and fee fields, and note the transaction size or weight. Under inputs, follow links to the referenced previous transactions to see which UTXOs funded the transaction. Under outputs, identify the likely recipient and the change output by reasoning about addresses and amounts. Confirm conservation of value by verifying that the sum of inputs equals the sum of outputs plus the fee. A useful reflection is to ask which output appears to be change and why — often change goes to an address controlled by the sender and may look similar to the sender's addresses. Finally, consider the fee per byte and whether that fee likely resulted in quick inclusion. This exercise ties the conceptual elements to a concrete explorer view and strengthens your ability to inspect transactions critically. screens.title: Assessment Questions and Explanations
screens.subtitle: Two formative questions to test understanding

narration.text: Use these assessment prompts to check your understanding of mempool behavior, fees, Merkle Trees, and transaction structure. First question: explain the mempool's role and how fees influence a transaction's journey from broadcast to being included in a block. A correct explanation will say that the mempool stores valid, unconfirmed transactions and that miners select transactions from their mempool to maximize fee revenue, prioritizing higher fee per byte during congestion. Second question: describe the purpose of a Merkle Tree within a block and how the Merkle Root supports efficient verification. A good answer describes hashing transactions into pairs up the tree until one root exists, and explains that the Merkle Root in the header lets lightweight clients verify inclusion with a small set of intermediate hashes. When writing answers, connect concepts: describe how fee pressure affects mempool size, and how Merkle proofs let you confirm inclusion without the full block. These prompts test whether you can explain both process and design rationale, not just recite definitions. Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Assessment Questions
Question 1
Role of the mempool and fees
Explain how the mempool stores unconfirmed transactions and why miners prioritize by fee per byte. Include what happens during high congestion.
Correct answers mention that miners select transactions to maximize fee income and that low-fee transactions can be delayed or dropped when mempools are full.
Question 2
Merkle Tree purpose
Describe how a Merkle Tree summarizes transactions and how a Merkle Root allows compact inclusion proofs for light clients.
A strong answer explains hashing leaves, combining pairs upward, and using Merkle paths to prove inclusion without full block download.
Key Takeaway

Answering process and rationale questions shows deeper understanding than simple definitions; connect steps to why they exist.

narration.text: Let's summarize three essential concepts from this chapter. First, a transaction is a signed message that transfers control of UTXOs from inputs to outputs; signatures authorize spending. Second, the mempool is the temporary holding area of unconfirmed transactions, and miners select from their mempool typically by fee per byte, so fees influence confirmation times. Third, miners package transactions into blocks constrained by size or weight limits and include a Merkle Root in the block header to summarize transactions efficiently. Each of these concepts ties to a practical skill: reading a TxID to find inputs and outputs, evaluating fees to predict inclusion likelihood, and understanding how a Merkle Root enables compact verification. When reviewing, focus on how these pieces connect — signatures ensure only rightful owners spend UTXOs, mempools queue validated transactions awaiting mining, and Merkle Trees let you prove inclusion without full data.

keyIdea.title: Remember
keyIdea.text: Transactions change ownership with signed inputs/outputs; mempool and fees determine selection; Merkle Root summarizes block transactions for efficient proofs.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Key Concepts — Part 1
Transaction
A signed record moving ownership of UTXOs via inputs and outputs.
Mempool
Nodes' temporary store of unconfirmed transactions awaiting mining.
Merkle Root
A single hash in the header that summarizes all block transactions.
Summary
Master these three concepts to read transactions, anticipate confirmation behavior, and verify inclusion efficiently.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 2
screens.subtitle: Three more ideas to keep in mind

narration.text: Finish with three additional key concepts. First, inputs reference previous UTXOs and require signatures produced by the private key controlling the UTXO. Second, outputs specify the recipient address and amount; change is simply another output back to the sender's control. Third, block size or weight limits combined with roughly ten-minute block intervals determine throughput and create the fee market that drives miner selection. These points tie back to practical activities: when you decode a transaction you will identify inputs and outputs, verify that signatures authorized spending, and calculate whether the fee makes sense for timely inclusion. Remember the common mistakes: don't equate addresses with accounts and don't assume broadcasting equals confirmation. Keeping these six compact concepts in your head will make reading explorers and reasoning about confirmations far more intuitive.

keyIdea.title: Final reminder
keyIdea.text: Inputs need signatures; outputs include change; limits plus block time create throughput constraints and fees.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Key Concepts — Part 2
Signature
Cryptographic proof authorizing spending of an input's UTXO.
Output
Destination address and amount; one output often represents change to the sender.
Block Size & Fees
Size limits plus block interval constrain throughput and create the fee market.
Final Takeaway
Combine transaction structure, mempool dynamics, and block packaging to reason about confirmations, fees, and verification with confidence.
